# Vectors in Postgres

![](../images/spot-2.svg){.spot fig-alt="A grid of white towers on a lime tile, with a violet ball floating above the yellow-topped one. An elephant in a lab coat inspects them with a magnifying glass."}
Semantic search represents each passage of text as an embedding (a vector of numbers) and answers a
question with the passages whose vectors lie closest to the question's.
[pgvector](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector) adds a `vector` type to Postgres, along with
distance operators and indexes, so the embeddings can live in the same table as the text, its
permissions and its foreign keys. A similarity search then becomes an ordinary `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`.

## Distance operators and opclasses

pgvector has four distance operators, and an index serves only queries that use the operator it was
built for, which is set by its operator class (opclass):

| SQL | SQLAlchemy | what it is | index opclass |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a <-> b` | `col.l2_distance(b)` | Euclidean distance | `vector_l2_ops` |
| `a <=> b` | `col.cosine_distance(b)` | 1 minus the cosine: 0 same direction, 2 opposite | `vector_cosine_ops` |
| `a <#> b` | `col.max_inner_product(b)` | the negative inner product (so smaller is closer) | `vector_ip_ops` |
| `a <+> b` | `col.l1_distance(b)` | taxicab distance | `vector_l1_ops` |

Most embedding models produce vectors of length 1, and for those cosine distance and inner product
rank results in the same order, with inner product saving a division. The notebook starts with a
dozen hand-made three-dimensional vectors whose axes mean something (`[fruit, tech, sport]`), so
that each distance can be worked out by hand before Postgres computes it.

## Similarity queries

A similarity query is a `SELECT` ordered by distance, and filters, joins and labels work around it
as in any other query:

```python
distance = Document.embedding.cosine_distance(query_vec).label("distance")
stmt = (
    select(Document.title, distance)
    .where(Document.category == "orm")  # ordinary filters first
    .order_by(distance)
    .limit(5)
)
```

Search systems often rerank the nearest results. A CTE takes the top 50 by vector distance, and the
outer query orders those 50 by a blended score (similarity with popularity or recency, for example)
or by a cross-encoder. To get the top results within each group,
`row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY distance)` numbers the rows in each category, and
the query keeps the first three of each.

## Re-embedding

An embedding pipeline runs again whenever its source text changes. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO
UPDATE` on a unique key handles both new and changed rows in one statement:

```python
stmt = insert(Document).values(rows)
stmt = stmt.on_conflict_do_update(index_elements=["name"], set_={"embedding": stmt.excluded.embedding})
```

## Approximate results

Without an index, Postgres computes the distance to every row and sorts them. The result is exact,
and the cost is acceptable up to some tens of thousands of rows. An approximate nearest-neighbor
index answers much faster by looking at only part of the table, so it can miss some of the true
nearest neighbors, and its settings decide how many.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Matching opclass and operator

An HNSW index built with `vector_l2_ops` is ignored by a query that orders by `<=>`, and the plan
falls back to a sequential scan without any warning. `EXPLAIN` shows which plan a query gets.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Filtering

HNSW collects `hnsw.ef_search` candidates first and applies `WHERE` afterwards. A filter that keeps
10% of rows discards most candidates, so the query can return fewer rows than its `LIMIT`.
pgvector 0.8 added iterative scans, which keep walking the graph until the limit is met, enabled
with `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order`.
:::

## The doc-search app

The lab's FastAPI app uses these queries to search the SQLAlchemy documentation. `app/ingest.py`
fetches 20 pages of the documentation, splits them by section into chunks of about 250 words, embeds
each chunk with `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` (384 dimensions, ONNX on the CPU), and stores the 407 rows
with an HNSW index.

`POST /ask` embeds the question, takes the five chunks closest by cosine distance, and builds an
extractive summary from their sentences, so each answer quotes its sources and nothing is
generated. Retrieval takes about 20 ms. The [sync and async scene](sqlalchemy.qmd#watching-it-happen)
shows these queries in flight, with the chunks laid out by a PCA of their embeddings.
